definition: Garish means gaudy — loud, clashing show in bad taste.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word garish. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know garish should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The stadium's new scoreboard felt garish in the century-old park, all strobing red against brick and ivy.
Bold is confident color that stops far short of garish — assured, not assaulting.
Flashy goes further than bold — it wants your attention — but stops short of garish, which crosses into eyesore.

Gaudy is the closest cousin — flashy, cheap-looking display, colors and glitter chosen to impress and failing. Garish adds assault: the colors don't just look cheap, they clash and shout until the eye actually winces. Gaudy misjudges taste; garish attacks it.

Tawdry is showy on top and shabby underneath — thin glitter with cheapness showing through it. Garish is about the visual assault itself: loud, clashing color in bad taste, however much it cost. A garish ballroom can cost millions; tawdry always smells of cheapness.

Because garish's ancestry is disputed — the staring-word gauren is only a likely parent, and that verb itself died out — no confirmed relatives survive in modern English. The word stands alone, as loud in the dictionary as the colors it describes.
Garish means gaudy — loud, clashing show in bad taste.
The landlord repainted the hallway in traffic-cone orange with mint-green trim, a combination so garish that tenants joked about needing sunglasses to collect the mail.
Garish is the right word because the colors don't just stand out — they clash, shout, and offend the eye.
Bold color used well is striking; color this loud and this graceless is garish, and the word passes judgment as it describes.
Garish condemns loud, clashing visual taste — neon on brick, sequins at a funeral.

Keep it apart from two neighbors in this unit: ornate measures how much decoration there is without necessarily disapproving, and lurid does for content what garish does for color — a poster's colors are garish, its gory details are lurid.

When the new owners reopened the boardwalk arcade, longtime visitors stopped short at the entrance.
The old hand-painted sign was gone, replaced by a wall of flashing panels in colors that fought one another for attention.
One reviewer wrote that the garish frontage 'doesn't invite the eye so much as ambush it,' and admitted she crossed the street to escape the glare.
The owners protested that nothing about the renovation was cheap; the panels were imported and the installation cost more than the building.
That, critics answered, was exactly the point: expense had never been the complaint.
The colors themselves were the assault.
